q: A plant disease is usually defined as abnormal growth and/or dysfunction of a plant.
e: This is the exact definition provided in the textbook.

q: Diseases are the result of some disturbance in the normal life process of the plant.
e: Plant diseases occur due to disturbances in normal physiological life processes.

q: Biotic diseases are caused by non-living environmental conditions.
e: Biotic diseases are caused by living organisms such as fungi, bacteria, and viruses.

q: Abiotic diseases are caused by non-living environmental conditions such as soil compaction, wind, and frost.
e: These are examples of non-living environmental factors that cause abiotic diseases.

q: Plant disease is any abnormal condition that alters the appearance or function of a plant.
e: This is a core definition of plant disease provided in the text.

q: Nematodes are very tiny roundworms that help distribute bacteria and fungi through the soil.
e: Nematodes act as plant parasites and assist in the distribution of other pathogens.

q: Infectious plant diseases are caused by a pathogenic organism such as a fungus, bacterium, mycoplasma, virus, viroid, nematode, or parasitic flowering plant.
e: These are the listed pathogenic organisms capable of causing infectious plant diseases.

q: An infectious agent is incapable of reproducing within or on its host.
e: An infectious agent is capable of reproducing within or on its host and spreading to others.

q: Non-infectious plant diseases are caused by unfavourable growing conditions and are not transmissible.
e: Because non-infectious agents cannot reproduce within a host, they cannot be transmitted.

q: The study of plant diseases is called plant pathology.
e: Plant pathology is explicitly defined as the study of plant diseases.

q: Pathology is derived from the two Greek words pathos (suffering, disease) and logos (discourse, study).
e: This is the etymological origin of the word pathology as stated in the text.

q: Biotic diseases can spread throughout one plant and also may spread to neighbouring plants of the same species.
e: Biotic diseases are transmissible and can spread to neighbouring susceptible plants.

q: Biotic diseases never show physical evidence (signs) of the pathogen.
e: Biotic diseases sometimes show physical evidence (signs) of the pathogen, such as fungal growth or bacterial ooze.

q: Abiotic diseases are caused by nonliving factors, such as drought stress, sunscald, and nutrient deficiency.
e: These are examples of nonliving factors that lead to abiotic diseases.

q: Abiotic damage does not spread from plant to plant over time.
e: Unlike biotic diseases, abiotic damage is not transmissible between plants.

q: Abiotic diseases frequently show the presence of disease signs.
e: Abiotic diseases do not show the presence of disease signs because they are not caused by living organisms.

q: Plant diseases occurrence and severity result from the impact of the host plant, the pathogen, and the environmental conditions.
e: These three factors make up the disease triangle.

q: Signs of plant disease are the visible effects of disease on the plant's reaction to the causal agent.
e: Symptoms are the visible effects of the plant's reaction; signs are the physical evidence of the pathogen itself.

q: Symptoms are visible effects of disease on plants, such as detectable changes in colour, shape, and/or functions.
e: This accurately describes symptoms of plant diseases.

q: Viruses cause mottling, spots, mosaic-like patterns, crinkling, and other malformations on leaves and fruits.
e: These are the characteristic symptoms caused by viral infections in plants.

q: Because viruses are systemic, infected plants can be easily cured with fungicides.
e: Because viruses are systemic, infected plants must be rogued or discarded; fungicides do not cure viruses.

q: Fungi and fungal-like organisms cause more plant diseases than any other group of plant pest.
e: Fungi and FLOs are responsible for the majority of plant diseases.

q: There are over $80,000$ species of fungi and fungal-like organisms shown to cause disease.
e: There are over $8,000$ species of fungi and fungal-like organisms shown to cause disease.

q: FLOs are organisms like Pythium and Phytophthora and cause downy mildew.
e: Pythium and Phytophthora are examples of fungal-like organisms that cause downy mildew.

q: Alternaria is a genus of fungi that causes rots of seeds.
e: Aspergillus causes rots of seeds; Alternaria causes leaf spots and blight of various plants.

q: Puccinia causes rust of cereals.
e: Puccinia is the fungal genus responsible for rust diseases in cereals.

q: Rhizopus causes soft rot of vegetables.
e: Rhizopus causes soft rot of fruits; Sclerotinia causes soft rot of vegetables.

q: There are approximately $200$ types of bacteria that cause diseases in plants.
e: While most bacteria are beneficial, about $200$ types are known to cause plant diseases.

q: Bacteria that cause plant diseases are most active in cold and dry environments.
e: Plant pathogenic bacteria are most active in warm and humid environments.

q: Most plant pathogenic bacteria belong to the genera Agrobacterium, Erwinia, Pseudomonas, Streptomyces and Xanthomonas.
e: These are the primary genera of bacteria known to cause plant diseases.

q: Nematodes are simple, multicellular animals and are bilaterally symmetrical, soft-bodied, non-segmented roundworms.
e: This is the exact biological description of nematodes provided in the text.

q: Most nematode species that attack plants are macroscopic.
e: Most nematode species that attack plants are microscopic.

q: Plant parasitic nematodes have a stylet, which is a piercing mouthpart.
e: The stylet is a key anatomical feature of plant parasitic nematodes.

q: The presence of a stylet is the key diagnostic sign differentiating plant parasitic nematodes from all other types of nematodes.
e: The stylet is the defining diagnostic feature for plant parasitic nematodes.

q: Biological control is the control of plant diseases using synthetic chemical compounds.
e: Biological control uses living microorganisms, not synthetic chemicals.

q: In biological control, an antagonist may secrete metabolites harmful to the pathogens, a mechanism known as antibiosis.
e: Antibiosis involves the secretion of harmful metabolites or antibiotics by the biological agent.

q: In biological control, competition occurs when an antagonist causes death of the parasite by producing enzymes.
e: Competition involves competing for nutrients or space; lysis involves causing death by producing enzymes.

q: Physical methods of disease prevention are based on the physiological tolerance of disease agents to adverse conditions.
e: Physical control exploits the limits of physiological tolerance of pathogens to factors like temperature or moisture.

q: Chemicals used to control bacteria are called fungicides.
e: Chemicals used to control bacteria are called bactericides; fungicides control fungi.

q: Chemicals used to control nematodes are called nematicides.
e: Nematicides are the specific chemical agents used to control nematode populations.

q: Abiotic diseases are caused by conditions external to the plant and are not due to living agents.
e: Abiotic diseases stem from non-living environmental and cultural factors.

q: The fungi that cause tomato leaf blight also cause severe damage on sweet corn.
e: Biotic diseases are often species-specific; the fungi causing tomato leaf blight do not damage sweet corn.

q: Non-infectious causal agents are organisms capable of reproducing within a host.
e: Non-infectious causal agents are not organisms and cannot reproduce within a host.

q: Biotic diseases are more limited to a certain species compared to abiotic damage.
e: Abiotic damage often affects many plant species, while biotic problems are usually limited to certain species.

q: Signs of plant disease include conks, fruiting bodies, mildew, mushrooms, and mycelium.
e: These are all physical examples of signs (the actual organisms or their structures).

q: Symptoms of disease include bacterial ooze and nematode cysts.
e: Bacterial ooze and nematode cysts are signs of disease, not symptoms.

q: Fusarium is a genus of fungi that causes root rot of many plants.
e: Fusarium is explicitly listed as causing root rot in many plants.

q: Sclerotinia causes soft rot of fruits.
e: Sclerotinia causes soft rot of vegetables; Rhizopus causes soft rot of fruits.

q: Botrytis causes blights of various plants.
e: Botrytis is a fungal genus known to cause blights in various plant species.

q: A disease is an illness or disorder of the body or mind that leads to poor health.
e: This is the foundational definition of a disease provided in the chapter.

q: Animal diseases can be divided into non-infectious diseases and infectious diseases.
e: This is the primary classification of animal diseases.

q: Non-infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread from one person to another.
e: Non-infectious diseases are not caused by pathogens and cannot spread from person to person.

q: Non-infectious diseases are caused by factors such as aging, genetics, malnutrition, lifestyle and environment.
e: These are the primary non-pathogenic factors that lead to non-infectious diseases.

q: Examples of non-infectious diseases include cardiovascular disease, cancer, and malaria.
e: Malaria is an infectious disease caused by a protist; cardiovascular disease and cancer are non-infectious.

q: Most cardiovascular disease starts with atheroma formation.
e: Atheroma formation is the initial step in the development of most cardiovascular diseases.

q: If the endothelium is damaged by high blood pressure, an inflammatory response occurs where red blood cells move into the area.
e: White blood cells, mostly macrophages, move into the area during the inflammatory response, not red blood cells.

q: White blood cells and lipids from the blood clump together under the endothelium to form fatty streaks.
e: This clumping forms the initial fatty streaks in the artery wall.

q: Over time, more white blood cells, lipids and connective tissue build up and harden to form a fibrous plaque called atheroma.
e: This describes the progression from fatty streaks to a hardened atheroma plaque.

q: An atheroma plaque partially blocks the lumen of the artery and restricts blood flow, which causes blood pressure to decrease.
e: The restriction of blood flow caused by the plaque causes blood pressure to increase.

q: The hardening of arteries, caused by atheroma, is called atherosclerosis.
e: Atherosclerosis is the medical term for the hardening of arteries due to atheroma.

q: In angina, plaques build up slowly in the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the parts of the heart muscle.
e: This reduced blood flow to the heart muscle is the underlying cause of angina.

q: During exercise, the narrowed coronary arteries cannot supply enough oxygenated blood and the heart muscle resorts to aerobic respiration.
e: The heart muscle resorts to anaerobic respiration when oxygenated blood supply is insufficient.

q: The symptoms of angina subside once exercise stops.
e: Angina pain typically subsides when the heart's demand for oxygen decreases upon resting.

q: Oxygen is supplied to the heart muscle by the pulmonary arteries.
e: Oxygen is supplied to the heart muscle by the coronary arteries.

q: If the coronary artery becomes completely blocked by a blood clot, an area of the heart muscle will be totally cut off from its blood supply.
e: Complete blockage leads to myocardial infarction due to total loss of blood supply.

q: Myocardial infarction is more commonly known as a stroke.
e: Myocardial infarction is more commonly known as a heart attack; a stroke affects the brain.

q: A stroke is caused by an interruption to the normal blood supply to an area of the brain.
e: This interruption, whether by blockage or bleeding, causes a stroke.

q: A blockage causing a stroke is usually caused by a blood clot, an atheroma or a combination of the two.
e: These are the primary physical causes of arterial blockages leading to strokes.

q: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of a blood clot in an artery deep inside the body.
e: DVT is the formation of a blood clot in a vein, not an artery.

q: DVT usually happens in arm veins and is caused by prolonged inactivity.
e: DVT usually happens in leg veins, often due to prolonged inactivity.

q: The three main non-modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease are genes, age, and gender.
e: These three factors cannot be changed and inherently affect CVD risk.

q: Women are more likely to suffer from heart disease than men.
e: Men are more likely to suffer from heart disease and other CVDs than women.

q: As a person gets older, the blood vessels begin to lose their elasticity and to narrow slightly.
e: This age-related change in blood vessels increases the likelihood of suffering from CVDs.

q: Smoking substances can damage the artery linings, which makes the build-up of plaques more likely.
e: Substances in tobacco smoke directly damage artery linings, promoting atheroma formation.

q: A sedentary lifestyle helps to prevent adverse health effects and lowers the risk of developing atherosclerosis.
e: A sedentary lifestyle leads to heart diseases; regular exercise helps prevent these adverse effects.

q: A healthy blood pressure is around $120 	ext{ mmHg}$ during systole and around $80 	ext{ mmHg}$ during diastole.
e: These are the standard healthy blood pressure values provided in the textbook.

q: If the blood pressure is regularly above $140/90 	ext{ mmHg}$, it is a sign of low blood pressure.
e: A reading regularly above $140/90 	ext{ mmHg}$ is a sign of high blood pressure or hypertension.

q: Being overweight is a very important indicator of risk for developing cardiovascular diseases.
e: While not always a direct cause, being overweight is a critical indicator and predictor of CVD risk.

q: Type 2 diabetes can result in damage to the lining of the blood vessels which increases the risk of plaque formation.
e: Damage to the blood vessel lining from type 2 diabetes directly promotes plaque formation.

q: A body mass index (BMI) of $18.5-25 	ext{ kg/m}^2$ is the ideal range for maintaining a healthy weight.
e: This is the ideal BMI range stated for preventing cardiovascular disease.

q: Antihypertensives drugs such as beta blockers and ACE inhibitors are prescribed to increase blood pressure.
e: Antihypertensive drugs are prescribed to reduce blood pressure.

q: Statins are a group of drugs used to lower the level of cholesterol in the blood.
e: Statins are specifically used to lower blood cholesterol levels and reduce atherosclerosis risk.

q: Statins improve the balance of HDLs to LDLs and reduce inflammation in the lining of the arteries.
e: Statins improve the balance of LDLs to HDLs (lowering the bad cholesterol relative to the good).

q: Plant stanols and sterols compounds reduce the levels of LDLs in the blood.
e: These compounds, found in certain foods, help reduce LDL levels.

q: Anticoagulants such as warfarin and heparin are used to increase blood clotting.
e: Anticoagulants are used to reduce blood clotting and prevent blockages.

q: Platelet inhibitory drugs such as aspirin prevent platelets from clumping together.
e: Aspirin acts as an anticoagulant by preventing platelets from clumping and forming clots.

q: Infectious diseases are sometimes called communicable diseases as they are passed from infected to uninfected people.
e: Communicable is another term for infectious diseases due to their transmissible nature.

q: The prevalence of a disease is the death rate from different diseases.
e: Prevalence is the number of people who have the disease at any one time; mortality is the death rate.

q: Diseases that are always in populations are described as endemic.
e: Endemic diseases maintain a constant presence within a specific population.

q: An epidemic occurs when there is a sudden increase in the number of people with a disease.
e: This sudden spike in cases defines an epidemic.

q: A pandemic occurs when there is an increase in the number of cases throughout a continent or across the world.
e: A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread over a massive geographic scale.

q: Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae, which is a virus.
e: Vibrio cholerae is a bacterium, not a virus.

q: Malaria is caused by four species of Plasmodium, which is a protist.
e: Plasmodium is a protist responsible for causing malaria.

q: HIV/AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, which is a bacterium.
e: HIV is a virus, not a bacterium.

q: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. bovis.
e: These two bacterial species are the causative agents of Tuberculosis.

q: The female Anopheles mosquito is a vector of malaria.
e: The female Anopheles mosquito transmits the Plasmodium parasite between humans.

q: Female Anopheles mosquitoes feed on human blood to obtain the carbohydrates they need to develop their eggs.
e: They feed on human blood to obtain the protein they need to develop their eggs.

q: Male and female gametes of Plasmodium fuse in the human's liver.
e: The gametes fuse in the mosquito's gut, not the human's liver.

q: The infective stages of Plasmodium pass from the mosquito's salivary glands into the human's blood.
e: The parasite is injected into the human bloodstream via the mosquito's saliva.

q: Quinine and chloroquine are anti-malarial drugs used to treat infected people.
e: These are standard anti-malarial drugs used for treatment and prophylaxis.

q: Chloroquine inhibits lipid synthesis and prevents the parasite spreading within the body.
e: Chloroquine inhibits protein synthesis, not lipid synthesis.

q: Proguanil inhibits the sexual reproduction of Plasmodium inside the biting mosquito.
e: This is the specific added advantage of Proguanil as a prophylactic drug.

q: Mefloquine is a drug used in South America, Africa and New Guinea that has no side-effects.
e: Mefloquine sometimes causes unpleasant side-effects such as restlessness and dizziness.

q: Artesunate is a drug derived from the plant compound artemisinin.
e: Artesunate is a plant-derived anti-malarial compound.

q: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in dry soil.
e: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in water, where the larvae hatch and develop.

q: Oil can be spread over the surfaces of water to make it impossible for mosquito larvae and pupae to breathe.
e: This physical control method suffocates the aquatic stages of the mosquito.

q: Mosquito fish Gambusia affinis feed on adult mosquitoes.
e: Mosquito fish feed on mosquito larvae in the water, not adult mosquitoes.

q: The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis kills mosquito larvae but is not toxic to other forms of life.
e: This biological control agent specifically targets mosquito larvae without harming other organisms.

q: In the 1950s, the World Health Organization (WHO) coordinated a worldwide eradication programme for malaria.
e: The WHO launched this global initiative in the 1950s.

q: The WHO eradication programme was generally successful because Plasmodium remained susceptible to all drugs.
e: The programme was not generally successful largely because Plasmodium became resistant to the drugs used.

q: Mosquitoes became resistant to dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane (DDT) and other insecticides like dieldrin.
e: Insecticide resistance was a major factor in the failure of early eradication efforts.

q: The whole genome of Plasmodium has been sequenced.
e: Sequencing the genome is a recent advance that may lead to effective vaccines.

q: Malaria may be transmitted during blood transfusion and when unsterile needles are re-used.
e: Though primarily vector-borne, the parasite can be transmitted via infected blood.

q: Plasmodium can pass across the placenta from mother to fetus.
e: Vertical transmission of malaria from mother to fetus is possible.

q: If people are continually re-infected by different strains of malaria they become immune, and this immunity lasts forever even if they leave the endemic area.
e: The immunity only lasts as long as people remain in contact with the disease in the endemic area.

q: The introduction of simple dip stick tests means that diagnosis of malaria can be done quickly without the need for laboratories.
e: Dip stick tests for malaria antigens allow for rapid, field-based diagnosis.

q: High blood pressure can be the result of atherosclerosis because the walls of the arteries become less flexible due to the build-up of plaques.
e: The loss of arterial flexibility from plaques directly causes blood pressure to rise.

q: Type 2 diabetes decreases the risk of plaque formation by protecting the lining of the blood vessels.
e: Type 2 diabetes increases the risk of plaque formation by damaging the lining of the blood vessels.
